We encode compact fractional viscoelastic models as causal convolutional features derived from the Boltzmann superposition principle, and we jointly fit multi-temperature chirp records using sparse variational Gaussian process regression. The model infers horizontal shift factors, constitutive parameters, and an observational-noise scale directly from time-domain stress-strain signals measured in the linear viscoelastic regime, without first extracting frequency-domain spectra or manually shifting separate curves. For synthetic Fractional Maxwell data, the method recovers the generating constitutive law from a prescribed model library and latent shifts over stress-noise levels from 3% to 25%. Applied to a DGEBA-IPDA epoxy dataset spanning the glass-transition regime, the pooled likelihood distinguishes competing fractional rheology models using the Bayesian information criterion. These results recast TTS master-curve construction as probabilistic inference over latent time rescaling and linear viscoelasticity, while also identifying limitations, such as homoscedastic noise and weakly informative spectral regimes.

title: Configuration-Independent Low-Energy Gaps in Graphene Nanoribbons: A $δ$-Scatterer Transfer-Matrix Approach
summary: Transport measurements on lithographically patterned graphene nanoribbons suggest that the gap depends primarily on ribbon width rather than on crystallographic edge orientation, in contrast to predictions of ideal tight-binding models. To address this, we develop a transfer-matrix approach, based on the theory of finite periodic systems, in which each carbon atom of the honeycomb lattice is represented by an individual $δ$-scatterer with interaction strength $γ^{}_δ$ and the nanoribbon is treated as a confined multichannel finite periodic system. We derive the unit-cell transfer matrix for both arm-chair and zig-zag edge configurations and obtain the transmission and channel-coupling coefficients in closed form. The transmission spectra display the resonant band structure characteristic of finite periodic systems, with the number of resonances per allowed band increasing with the number of unit cells. For $γ_δ=0$ the ribbons are fully transparent; for $γ_δ>0$ a low-energy transport gap opens and grows linearly with the scatterer strength, $Δ=0.364265\,γ_δ$, identically for arm-chair and zig-zag edges. These results are consistent with the reported absence of a systematic dependence on orientation, while the analytical results show that interchannel coupling vanishes exactly for arm-chair ribbons and decreases with increasing width for zig-zag ribbons, revealing the role of edge geometry. Together, these findings indicate that atomic-scale scattering, represented by the $δ$-potential formalism, provides a common orientation-independent contribution to the low-energy transport gap in the pristine ribbons considered here.

title: Rationalizing charge transfer: a single-molecule case study across three distinct surfaces
summary: Organic molecules are versatile building blocks for the formation of complex low-dimensional nanostructures on surfaces. Recently, interest has grown in translating on-surface synthetic protocols from noble metal surfaces to insulating surfaces, which offer technological relevance, and to magnetic or superconducting surfaces, which offer new routes to correlated phases. It is important, therefore, to understand how these alternative surfaces may alter the properties of adsorbates through processes like charge transfer and screening. Evidence for charge transfer is often obtained experimentally via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), and theoretically via density functional theory (DFT). In this work, we systematically compare the properties of isolated macrocyclic emeraldine (Me$_6$) molecules on three different surfaces: metallic Au(111), a semiconducting ferromagnetic monolayer of FeCl$_2$, and a cleaved superconducting surface of bulk 2H-NbSe$_2$. We show that STS and DFT alone are insufficient to quantify charge transfer for these cases. Instead, we complement these methods with Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) measurements and model Hamiltonian calculations to demonstrate that on Au(111) and FeCl$_2$, Me$_6$ molecules donate a single electron to the substrate, whereas on NbSe$_2$ two electrons are transferred from molecule to substrate. Our work provides insight into the interplay of charge transfer, screening, and molecule-substrate coupling, and develops experimental and theoretical methods for comparing the properties of adsorbates across different surfaces for future studies.

title: Combining Simulations and Spectroscopy to Design Protective Coatings on Sulfide Solid Electrolytes
summary: Sulfide solid electrolytes are attractive for all-solid-state batteries because of their high Li-ion conductivity and favorable processability, but their practical use is limited by electrochemical instability and moisture-induced degradation. Molecular surface coatings offer a scalable strategy to improve humidity tolerance and interfacial stability, yet there is limited understanding of the molecular-level factors governing surface interactions. By combining large-scale atomistic simulations enabled by a machine-learning potential with targeted experiments, we present a comprehensive framework for designing molecular coatings on Li$_6$PS$_5$Cl (LPSCl). Using a PET-MAD interatomic potential fine-tuned on an r$^2$SCAN reference dataset covering LPSCl surfaces, molecular adsorbates, and their interactions, we model surface adsorption of carboxylic (CA), sulfonic (SA), and phosphonic (PA) acids with alkyl chains of varying lengths and the interaction of these coated surfaces with water at finite temperature. The simulations show that lithiated head groups generally exhibit more favorable adsorption energies. Impedance spectroscopy shows that the lithiated coatings maintain 40--55\% of the initial ionic conductivity after powder processing. While adsorption strength is largely controlled by head-group chemistry and lithiation state, coating morphology depends primarily on alkyl-chain length and surface coverage. In particular, long-chain lithiated carboxylates form dense, brush-like hydrophobic layers that reduce water access to reactive Li surface sites, with protection setting in at a coating thickness of approximately 0.8 nm. Consistent with these predictions, longer carboxylate chains suppress H$_2$S evolution more effectively. Because thicker coatings also hinder Li-ion transport, intermediate chain lengths offer the best balance between moisture protection and ionic conductivity.

title: Folding of Free Polymers Under Confinement by Responsive Hydrogels
summary: Controlling the folding of biopolymers in crowded and confined environments, such as the interior of biological cells, remains a significant challenge. Macromolecular crowding and spatial confinement can strongly influence transition pathways between folded and unfolded states of proteins. Such environments can be mimicked in experiments by confining polymers within soft, tunable media, such as hydrogels -- cross-linked polymer networks that swell by absorbing solvent and exhibit stimulus-dependent responsiveness. Here, we develop a self-consistent mean-field theory for the equilibrium swelling and internal composition of a hydrogel immersed in a solution of free polymer coils. The theory extends the Flory-Rehner framework by incorporating free polymer coils, modeled as fluctuating ellipsoids, whose sizes and shapes are characterized by the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor. Confinement of the coils within gel pores is characterized by an effective free-volume fraction, parametrized from numerical calculations for self-avoiding-walk chains between hard walls. Coupled chemical potential equilibrium conditions are solved numerically over ranges of coil molecular weight and free polymer concentration. We find that free polymers drive a non-monotonic swelling response of hydrogels, with osmotic swelling at low concentrations followed by deswelling at higher concentrations, in qualitative agreement with experiment. We further demonstrate that confinement within gel pores reduces the radius of gyration and asphericity of embedded polymer coils, driving them toward compact, globular conformations analogous to folded protein states. These results establish a theoretical foundation for using responsive hydrogels as tunable, artificial chaperone-like systems capable of inducing and controlling biopolymer folding.

title: CO2-Induced Shifts in the Confined Phase Transformation of CH4 in Metal-Organic Frameworks
comment: Supplemental Information and Input files available upon request. Under review (ACS Omega)
summary: A sharp increase in gas uptake over a narrow pressure range can occur for fluids confined in nanoporous materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), reflecting a transformation between distinct adsorption states, often accompanied by the existence of metastable states. Understanding how co-adsorbed species modify this behavior is important for predicting and optimizing gas storage and separation. Here, we investigate the effect of CO2 on the adsorption transformation of confined CH4 in rigid IRMOF-1 and IRMOF-8. Transition-Matrix Monte Carlo (TMMC) simulations were performed for systems containing 0-75 and 0-150 CO2 molecules in IRMOF-1 and IRMOF-8, respectively. While the addition of CO2 decreases the maximum CH4 uptake, consistent with competition for pore space, remarkably, the presence of CO2 significantly shifts the discontinuity in the CH4 adsorption isotherm to substantially lower pressures relative to the pure CH4 system. This promotion of the high-density CH4 phase at lower pressures demonstrates that CO2 substantially alters the thermodynamic landscape governing confined CH4 through changes in both fluid-fluid and fluid-framework interactions. These results establish CO2 as a thermodynamic modifier of confined CH4 behavior and suggest that controlled co-adsorption provides a means of tuning adsorption transformations in nanoporous materials.

title: Extended Hydrodynamics of Planar Heisenberg Ferromagnetic Systems
summary: Access to hydro and quasi-hydro regimes in magnetic systems is steadily increasing with the advances in fabrication of clean materials, and motivates study of hydrodynamics beyond conventional regimes and probe non-equilibrium transport. We employ the framework of extended irreversible thermodynamics which includes dynamical dissipative currents as quasi-hydro variables, and effect the modified hydrodynamic equations suitable to describe planar Heisenberg ferromagnetic systems in both paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. We show that the new transport coefficients and relaxation time scales introduced by quasi-hydro variables can engineer diverse combination of dispersion relations and provide control over the nature of hydrodynamic modes. For instance, we can change the diffusive energy mode into propagating one in multiple ways, including by tuning the relaxation time of magnetization current.

title: Vacancy-enhanced Li solid-solution anodes for solid-state batteries: computational screening enabling high critical current density
summary: Sluggish vacancy-mediated self-diffusion in lithium metal limits the critical current density (CCD) of Li anodes in solid-state batteries by promoting interfacial void formation during stripping. To enhance the effective vacancy concentration while preserving the bcc Li host, we screen 50 substitutional solutes using density functional theory (DFT) within a funnel based on automatic phase diagram construction, solution energies, solute-vacancy binding energies, and experimental solubility limits. Using an adaptation of the Lomer model for the dilute limit, we show that only Ag, Ge, and Cd solid solutions are predicted to reach $1~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ within their solubility limits. The thermodynamically estimated CCD of Ag at $\sim 9$ at.% reaches $\sim 4~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ at a theoretical capacity of $1522~\mathrm{mAh~g^{-1}}$. Migration barrier calculations indicate that the enhancement may be partially offset by vacancy trapping, necessitating further validation via molecular dynamics simulations. Notably, Hume-Rothery rules alone prove insufficient as prefilters, whereas machine-learning models trained on the DFT data can eliminate most unsuitable solutes early in the funnel and extend the workflow to related solid-solution searches.

title: Robustness of Skyrmion-Mediated Magnetization Switching in Perpendicular Magnetic Tunnel Junctions (p-MTJs) to Material Disorder and Elevated Temperature
summary: Transient-skyrmion mediated voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy (VCMA) switching is a fast and energy efficient way to magnetization reversal, but its reliability under realistic material disorder and thermal fluctuations remain unclear. In this work, we use stochastic micromagnetic simulations of a 100 nm perpendicular magnetic tunnel junction to study switching reliability under grain-scale variations in Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, easy-axis orientation, and intergrain exchange coupling. We find that switching remains robust under moderate disorder, with 100% switching observed in 10^4 stochastic simulations after pulse width optimization at both 300 K and 350 K. Increasing the temperature from 300 to 350 K shifts the optimum VCMA pulse width from ~475 to ~450 ps, indicating that an apparent reduction in switching probability at a fixed pulse duration can be primarily due to pulse detuning. In contrast, strong easy-axis disorder reduces the maximum switching probability even after pulse-width optimization, indicating degradation of the switching dynamics. We further show that, under strong easy-axis disorder a transient skyrmion still forms while the subsequent post-pulse dynamics fails to complete the magnetization reversal. Our study therefore establishes the distinction between recoverable reliability due to timing shifts and permanent disorder-induced degradation that simply cannot be recovered by pulse re-tuning. Finally, for no disorders but at room temperature, 100% switching is observed with 10^6 stochastic simulations with correct pulse shaping.

title: Free energy fluctuations of symmetric perceptron models up to and including criticality
summary:
We study the free energy fluctuations of spherical and Ising perceptron models with general even activations. These include the symmetric binary perceptron, the $U$-perceptron, and the bipartite Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model. Our main result is a Gaussian CLT for the free energy that holds both in the ``high-temperature'' interior of a second moment RS regime and on its ``critical'' boundary. At criticality, the CLT has scale $(\frac{\log N}{6})^{1/2}$, which matches the free energy fluctuations of the critical Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model and suggests this scaling is universal.
  The proof shows that the perceptron model's free energy fluctuations are explained, up to an additive $o(1)$ error with high probability, by those of a corresponding spherical Hopfield model, and that this relation persists even at criticality. This proof strategy builds on a critical reweighted moment method developed by the first and third authors \cite{du2026fluctuations} to identify the critical fluctuations of the SK free energy, which links these fluctuations to the spectral edge spacing of the disorder.

title: Intertwining Defects and Fermion-Boundary Scattering from TQFT
summary: We construct conformal boundary conditions of free Dirac fermions that preserve chiral, anomaly-free symmetries, and determine the associated fermion-boundary scattering, using the TQFT/CFT framework. We apply the construction to several previously unresolved examples: higher-charge monopoles in non-chiral QED, a family of $SU(N)\times SU(N+2)$-symmetric models, the chiral QED with charges $\{1^5,3,(-2)^4\}$, and the charge-three monopole of the Standard Model. In these examples, out-going states are created by defect operators at the end of non-invertible topological lines; when such a line is non-simple, the out-going state splits into superselection sectors, and we give a formula for the branching ratios in terms of TQFT data. We also propose a general construction that adds and then gaps neutral spectators, under a technical assumption, which is potentially applicable to the 1-5-7-8-9 model.

title: Quantum Complexity and Stabilizer-State Expansions: From Pairing to Deformation in Fermionic Systems
summary: Understanding how collective phenomena such as pairing and deformation emerge in interacting fermionic systems, and how the correlations underlying them shape the resources required for their simulation, is a central challenge in many-body physics. We investigate various aspects of quantum complexity in a fermionic system exhibiting two main forms of collectivity, specifically deformation and pairing, through entanglement, non-stabilizerness, and fermionic non-Gaussianity. In the deformed phase, high entanglement coexists with low non-stabilizerness, while the superfluid pairing phase, by contrast, exhibits substantial multipartite entanglement and non-stabilizerness, together with maximal fermionic anti-flatness. In a second step we examine how to describe the phase diagram of the system in a classically scalable and symmetry-preserving way, by combining stabilizer-state expansion and variational basis optimization. A physics-guided decomposition of the Hamiltonian identifies the relevant stabilizer states, which can be constructed from graph states. A single stabilizer state captures the deformed phase to a large extent, and, although the number of stabilizer states required to describe the pairing phase grows exponentially with system size, a symmetry-preserving basis rotation yields a high-fidelity approximation using far fewer states. This rotated state can then serve as a practical starting point for quantum refinement.

title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows
summary: Conventional particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) has been the standard diagnostic tool for studying fluid and granular flows. However, in dense granular systems, the average distance moved by particles between frames can approach or exceed inter-particle spacing, demanding ultra-high frame rates. Furthermore, neighbouring particles may move together, and common velocity-based prediction fails after energetic collisions. Existing methods struggle to track granular particles without losing identities or swapping. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV), a training-free multi-pass method leveraging multicoloured particles to achieve enhanced tracking. CBTV first matches constellations of neighbouring coloured particles as single units, guided by a cross-correlation motion prior, and only then assigns the remaining particles individually. We compare it with 12 baseline tracker configurations, from classical linkers to graph-neural-network and transformer models, on 59 cases from 15 simulated discrete-element granular flows with exact ground truth (0.006-9 diameters/frame). CBTV matches or exceeds every tracker tested on an impulsive collision at every displacement. Its advantage lies in dense flows in which particles move between about half and twice their spacing per frame, where links between frames are ambiguous. On agitated shear flow, a colour relaxation tracker, which also uses neighbour context, matches or narrowly exceeds CBTV. Where links are unambiguous, CBTV is close to the best tracker, and beyond about two to three particle diameters per frame, the range of its motion prior, trackers that compensate for bulk motion are more accurate. For experimentalists, dense granular flows of coloured particles can be tracked at displacements per frame where trackers without neighbour context lose identities, easing the demand for ultra-high frame rates without training data.

title: QuantumMatterExplorer: An Autonomous Agent for the Discovery of Quantum Many-Body Phases of Matter
comment: 42 pages, 10 figures and 3 tables in the main manuscript. Includes a 13-page agent-generated research note
summary: Mapping the phase diagram of a new quantum Hamiltonian demands expert judgement at every step: which observables to measure, where in parameter space to compute, or how to separate genuine order from finite-size artefacts. We introduce QuantumMatterExplorer, an autonomous agent that takes only a Hamiltonian and its parameter ranges as input and returns a phase diagram obtained from its own numerical simulations. The agent is built on a large language model and is designed to reason over a long horizon, maintain a persistent written plan, and drive a set of computational tools, with density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations cross-checked against independent exact diagonalization. The agent combines a large language model with persistent planning, a library of expert computational-physics skills, and density-matrix renormalization group calculations validated against independent exact diagonalization. It adaptively selects quantities to evaluate, refines parameter scans, and performs finite-size analyses as evidence accumulates. After validating the approach on Hamiltonians with known transitions, we challenge it with a frustrated bilinear-biquadratic spin-1 chain with single-ion anisotropy, whose two-dimensional phase diagram was published only recently and is unlikely to appear in any training corpus. Given no hint about the expected physics, the agent proposes which observables to probe, and identifies candidate Néel, Haldane and dimerized phases, in broad agreement with the reference phase diagram. It also detects incommensurate correlations and infers the frustration-dependent geometry of the phase boundaries, all within an eight-hour compute budget. These results open a practical route to the autonomous computational discovery of new phases of quantum matter.

title: Conviction versus Conformity in a Random-Field Ising Electorate: Antagonistic Ties, Network Density, and a Parameter-Free Prediction
summary: We study the zero-temperature random-field Ising model with +-J bond disorder on sparse graphs as a model of an electorate: survey-derived, trimodal fields compete with social couplings, a fraction alpha of which are antagonistic. With exact ground states up to N=180 (over 78000 optimizations, certified except in the densest frustrated cases) and validated heuristics to N=720, we locate the crossover r_h* at which the field carries half of the ground-state energy, close to where half the voters held against their own field have switched (0.93 r_h* for alpha<=0.2). Our main test is a zero-temperature cavity theory solved on the graph ensemble with no fitted parameter: at seven densities not otherwise used, predicted before their exact ground states were computed, it placed r_h* within 10% in 19 of 21 cells (median error 3%). Its errors are unsigned at alpha=0.05 and 0.5 but all negative at alpha=0.2, where it predicts the coupling energy correctly but a crossover that is early and, at high density, too sharp, and where its replica-symmetric solution is unstable in six of seven cells, consistent with replica-symmetry breaking at intermediate frustration. Empirically r_h*~0.91 e_J(0), with e_J(0) the coupling energy of the zero-field ground state, inside a rigorous per-instance factor-of-two window, so the known +-J energy laws carry over: r_h* ~ <k>^gamma with gamma=1.01-1.09 for alpha=0.05 and 0.50-0.57 for alpha>=0.5 (<k>=3-28; five graph families agree at matched density). At intermediate frustration r_h* is not a power law: sparse networks accommodate antagonistic ties at the cost of cooperative ones, which stops paying near <k>~10; the theory reproduces this without adjustment. In weakly frustrated dense networks the ground state is a near-consensus following the sign of the aggregate field in 93-100% of realisations at small r_h, against near-chance agreement in frustrated ones.

title: Cross-coupled photon avalanche drives room-temperature intrinsic optical bistability
summary: Optically bistable materials promise technological advances in optical information processing, memristive devices, and multiparametric sensing. However, optical bistability is predominantly observed under cryogenic conditions or is governed by subtle thermo-optical nonlinearities. Here, we report on Ho3+-activated nanocrystals that exhibit cavity-free intrinsic optical bistability (IOB) at ambient conditions. Non-thermal IOB stems from a cross-coupled photon avalanche (XPA) mechanism enabled by a low-phonon-energy double-perovskite host, which reduces nonradiative losses and facilitates excited-state population via XPA, even when the pump intensity is below threshold. Time-resolved luminescence measurements support the proposed XPA, as evidenced by a double-rise profile consistent with two reservoir states interlocked in energy looping. IOB with high-contrast photoswitching (up to 46 dB) is observed at room temperature across multiple visible emission lines, enabling wavelength-division multiplexing and compatibility with common detectors. IOB is preserved across nano- to microscale crystals and different double-perovskite compositions, broadly enabling information photonics and advanced sensing.

title: Near-field maps of topological edge states of molecular aggregates
summary: Self-assembled two-dimensional molecular aggregates provide a versatile platform for engineering excitonic states, including topologically nontrivial edge states. However, these edge-states are difficult to probe optically: they have weak far-field transition strengths, and far-field spectra do not reveal whether an excitation is localized at the edge. For an aggregate consisting of two sublattices of molecules with genuinely complex transition dipoles, we show that spatially resolved near-field spectroscopy encodes the full spatial structure of these states. The resulting near-field maps do not mirror the site populations, but instead exhibit strongly nonuniform, interference-like features. We demonstrate that a convolutional neural network can reconstruct the complex expansion coefficients of the eigenstates from these maps, and that this reconstruction is robust against substantial random noise.

title: From Heterogeneity to Function: Enhanced Modular Dynamic Range in Hierarchical Brain Networks
summary: Hierarchical and modular organization defines brain architecture, yet how it supports flexible computation and functional specialization remains unclear. Although dynamic range is a hallmark of efficient information processing, its distribution across modules and hierarchical levels remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that hierarchical-modular networks naturally generate heterogeneous modular dynamics and firing rates, extending regimes of critical-like dynamics with enhanced intrinsic timescales, reflecting critical slowing down, and diverse scaling exponents without fine-tuning near criticality. Intrinsic timescales increase across hierarchical levels, while their dispersion within levels emerges only when connectivity profiles and firing rates are heterogeneous. We introduce modular dynamic range to quantify how individual modules respond to external inputs and show that heterogeneity enhances both global and module-specific sensitivity, with modular intrinsic timescales increasing with dynamic range. Local stimulation reduces dynamic range in homogeneous networks but enhances it in heterogeneous networks relative to global stimulation. Moreover, selectively stimulating intermediate hierarchical levels maximizes both global and modular dynamic range, revealing a principle of functional specialization. In heterogeneous networks, modular dynamic range is more variable and increases even in unstimulated modules, demonstrating distributed computational benefits beyond directly stimulated regions. Together, these findings establish heterogeneity as a mechanism through which hierarchical-modular networks sustain critical-like dynamics, generate hierarchical timescales, and distribute computational sensitivity, providing a basis for functional specialization without fine-tuning to criticality.

title: Multi-scale patterns arising from competing chemotactic interactions
summary: Classical chemotaxis models consider the directed motion of cells in response to a chemical gradient. Recent experiments suggest that biological microswimmers such as bacteria can perform chemotaxis toward multiple chemicals, which dynamically evolve depending on the distribution of the microswimmers. In this Letter, we consider a mass-conserving chemotaxis model in which pattern formation is driven by two competing chemicals, autoinducers and nutrients, where the former acts as an activator and the latter as an inhibitor for coarsening. We show that this can give rise to diverse patterns including long wavelength uninterrupted coarsening, Turing-like arrested coarsening, traveling waves as well as a novel class of mixed multi-scale oscillatory coarsening patterns, where a dense aggregate coexist with a dynamically spreading part of the population. We analytically derive the conditions for the onset of such patterns and discuss their physical implications, which significantly broadens our understanding of signaling active matter and pattern formation in general.

title: Approximating the Gibbs Measure of Spherical Spin Glasses to Within $o(N^{-1/2})$ in the Replica Symmetric Phase
comment: Companion paper to the paper Sampling from Spherical Spin Glasses in Total Variation via Algorithmic Stochastic Localization (arXiv:2404.15651) by the same authors
summary: We study the magnetization vector of mixed spherical spin glasses in a weak external field, in the replica symmetric phase. We derive a coordinatewise expansion of the magnetization which includes the leading cubic correction to the quadratic approximation, with an error that is $o(N^{-1/2})$ per coordinate. We also prove a corresponding high-moment bound for the full vector. Finally, our companion paper applies these estimates to the effective Hamiltonian obtained by restricting a tilted spherical spin glass to a narrow band around a TAP critical point. The resulting sharp approximation is designed for applications in which normalized Wasserstein accuracy is insufficient, including total-variation sampling by stochastic localization.

title: Entanglement Asymmetry and Asymmetry Contour under Boundary Symmetry Breaking
summary: We investigate how symmetry-breaking boundary magnetic fields affect magnetization and Rényi-2 entanglement asymmetry (EA) in the transverse-field Ising model. For the ground state, magnetization exhibits qualitatively distinct behaviors in the ordered and disordered phases. EA also exhibits phase-dependent behavior, which is well captured by the lower and upper bounds derived in this work. In the critical regime, both magnetization and EA exhibit behavior qualitatively consistent with the field-theoretical predictions for a related setup. We also study boundary-quench dynamics and find that magnetization propagates from the boundary into the bulk with a velocity consistent with the maximum quasiparticle velocity. In contrast, because EA is a subsystem-integrated quantity, its spatial structure is not directly resolved. We therefore introduce the asymmetry contour, a contour-like finite-difference quantity that provides a spatially resolved characterization of the symmetry-breaking information encoded in the reduced density matrix. The resulting contour is complementary to the local magnetization, retaining sensitivity to nonlocal many-body correlations while its dynamics also reflects the underlying quasiparticle propagation. These results show how EA and its contour can provide complementary information-theoretic characterizations of symmetry breaking and its spatial structure.

title: Neural LoFi with Backward Coupling: A Spectral Theory of Cross-Layer Feature Learning
summary: During joint training, backpropagation allows later layers to reshape earlier representations, a feedback mechanism absent from purely layer-wise learning. We extend Neural Low-Degree Filtering (Neural LoFi), a recently proposed layer-wise spectral surrogate for feature learning, to capture this interaction. Starting from the exact backpropagation gradients, we derive a local coupling between a neuron's incoming weights and its corresponding next-layer column. In a controlled small-initialization regime with smooth activations and fixed surroundings, these dynamics amplify singular modes of a cross-layer correlation operator. Each growing mode pairs an earlier feature with an upper-layer response through shared neuron coefficients. This motivates a backward-coupling algorithm in which upper-layer sensitivities generate sample-dependent effective labels for earlier spectral steps, while corrected features refine upward transmission. A function-space variational principle characterizes the selected feature-response pairs by maximizing the label correlation of their product under kernel-norm constraints. For three-layer networks, we derive self-consistent continuous-time dynamics for the filtered hidden-layer features, the activation kernels, and the network output under the proposed backward coupling. In a hierarchical multi-index model, we establish a feature-recovery separation: backward coupling recovers lower-layer directions invisible to the original forward label-weighted statistic. The linear specialization recovers residual-dependent singular-mode dynamics, while paired modes provide a dynamical mechanism for linked low-rank covariance components consistent with the rainbow-network picture. Experiments with fully connected and convolutional networks on binary CIFAR-10 show improved accuracy over forward Neural LoFi at matched widths.

title: Non-singlets and the phase diagram of Matrix Quantum Mechanics
summary: The quantum mechanics of one $N\times N$ Hermitian matrix in the infinite $N$ limit is well known to define a two-dimensional string theory when the quartic coupling constant $g$ is tuned to a special negative value $g_*$. We study the thermodynamics of this Matrix Quantum Mechanics (MQM), treating the SU$(N)$ symmetry as a global symmetry. Crucially, the non-singlets, i.e. states in non-trivial representations of SU$(N)$, implement the effects of vortices on the discretized worldsheets. This random lattice model has the low-temperature $c=1$ and high-temperature $c=0$ phases, with the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition separating them. We map out the phase diagram in the coupling--temperature plane, which is separated by the critical stability curve $T_c(g)$ extending from $g_*< g <0$. We study this curve using the non-perturbative matrix bootstrap and low- and high-temperature perturbation theory, which explain the thermal instability. At low temperatures, thermally excited non-singlets backreact on the Fermi sea of matrix eigenvalues, causing it to spill over. At high temperatures, the theory is described by an effective matrix integral obtained by dimensional reduction on the thermal circle; the eigenvalue distribution of the zero mode becomes unstable at the critical coupling. We conjecture that the BKT transition occurs at a special point on the critical curve and estimate its position. Finally, we switch to the regular square lattice and study the MQM-inspired Villain model, where the link factor is the one-dimensional propagator on a circle. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we map out the BKT transition in this model.

title: Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
summary: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.

title: Ideal interaction dynamics of defects and background fields in condensed matter
summary: While defect dynamics in condensed matter systems is widely studied and several methods are available to track the defect position over time, the formulation of dynamical models for the coupled evolution of both defect and background field quantities seems to be more challenging. Yet, the overall behavior of a system containing moving defects is strongly influenced by this defect-field interaction. Here, we propose a modeling framework for the conservative coupled evolution of the defect density and the background fields upon focusing on two relevant cases of study: the Gross-Pitaevskii theory of quantum fluids and the Ericksen-Leslie model of nematic liquid crystals. To achieve the coupled evolution, we combine the Euler-Poincaré variational setting of continuum dynamics with the gauge theory of topological defects. While the latter allows us to overcome certain ambiguities in definition of the defect density, the Euler-Poincaré method provides a unified modeling approach in the absence of defect reconnection.
